$$
\operatorname{log}⁡({c}^{m})=m\operatorname{log}⁡(c)
$$

Using the power rule for logarithms, the given expression can be rewritten as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{log}⁡\sqrt{6x} & =\operatorname{log}⁡((6x)^{1/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{log}⁡(6x)\end{aligned}

Hence, $p=\frac{1}{2}.$

canonical_examples.problem: By expressing $\ln\left(x^2\right)$ in the form $k\ln x,$ determine the value of $k.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the power rule for logarithms:

$$
\log_n(c^m)= m\log_n\left( c \right)
$$

Using the power rule for logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}) & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $k =2.$

Example: 
                    Evaluating an Expression Using the Power Rule
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the power rule for natural logarithms:

$$
\ln\left( c^m \right) = m\ln{c}
$$

Using the power rule for logarithms and the information given, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}) & =3\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(x) \\  & =3\cdot 0.2 \\  & =0.6.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The **power rule** allows us to simplify logarithms of exponentiated expressions. It states that

$$
\log_{n}\left( c^{\color{blue}m} \right) = {\color{blue}m}\log_{n}{c}.
$$

In other words, the logarithm has the effect of "bringing down the power."

For example, let's use the rule to simplify $\log\left(125\right)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{log}⁡(125) & =\operatorname{log}⁡({5}^{3}) \\  & =3\operatorname{log}⁡(5)\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** To understand why the power rule works, notice that we can reach the same result using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{log}⁡(125) & =\operatorname{log}⁡({5}^{3}) \\  & =\operatorname{log}⁡(5\cdot 5\cdot 5) \\  & =\operatorname{log}⁡(5)+\operatorname{log}⁡(5)+\operatorname{log}⁡(5) \\  & =3\operatorname{log}⁡(5)\end{aligned}
$$

The power rule is just a shortcut for the above procedure.
